V01.answer: Yes, you should report. The village's written rules treat a non-Hindu visitor living here as a tamiu (a non-member guest), and ask you to report to the banjar's administrators (prajuru) within one wuku, that is seven days of arriving, and then to pay the monthly community contribution (sadana krama) that each banjar sets for itself. You are also expected to share in the community's customary obligations in good and bad times. Do it early and through your landlord — they know which banjar your house belongs to and who to speak to.
V01.why_it_matters: Reporting and paying the small monthly dues is how newcomers are folded into banjar life here — it makes you known to your neighbours and shares the cost of ceremonies and upkeep, instead of you staying a stranger on the street.
recommended_actions: Ask your landlord which banjar your rented house belongs to and who the kelian (banjar head) is.
Go and report in person within your first week, bringing your passport and rental agreement.
Ask what the monthly contribution is and how it is paid, and keep a note of each payment.

Pendatang non-Hindu melapor ke prajuru dinas dalam satu wuku, lalu membayar iuran bulanan sesuai ketentuan banjar (lingkungan setempat). Teks aturan ini berasal dari naskah 2012, jadi rincian seperti besaran iuran sebaiknya Anda tanyakan langsung ke banjar tempat Anda tinggal.

V03.answer: Yes — in Canggu the household you live in is expected to sort its own rubbish before it goes out. The village's waste rule, a pararem (a village customary regulation), covers visitors and temporary residents, not only registered villagers. In practice that means keeping five separate bins for different kinds of waste, keeping organic scraps apart from plastic, paper, metal, glass and leftovers, cutting back on single-use plastic, and passing sellable recyclables to the banjar's (neighbourhood council's) waste group on their collection day, with the rest left out for the village collection. Villa staff usually know the routine, so ask them how it works where you stay.
V03.why_it_matters: Waste is a visible, shared worry here — a clean street and beach reflect respect for the banjar that hosts you, and everyone in the household is asked to help.
recommended_actions: Set up five separate bins in your villa and label them clearly
Rinse and separate plastic, paper, metal and glass from food scraps
Ask your villa manager which day the banjar waste group collects recyclables
Avoid single-use plastic bags and bottles where you can

(1) Setiap Krama Adat, Krama Tamiu, dan Tamiu dalam rumah tangga wajib melakukan pengelolaan sampah yang dihasilkannya.

V05.answer: If you don't sort your rubbish properly, the customary village's waste service can simply stop collecting from you. That is the sanction written into Canggu's village waste rule, and it applies to visitors and newcomers like you, not only to registered village members. So it is less a fine and more a practical consequence: no collection until you sort. Separately, for things like dumping waste in a river, ditch or on the street, burning rubbish, or leaving it piling up in the open, the rule sets out escalating steps: a friendly word on the spot, then a warning, and for repeated cases a customary penalty decided by the village elders themselves.
V05.why_it_matters: Waste here flows into rivers, springs and temple grounds that people treat as sacred, so sorting your rubbish is part of respecting the place you're living in.
recommended_actions: Separate organic waste from plastic, glass and paper before collection day.
Ask your accommodation host or landlord how collection works on your street and when to put bins out.
Never burn rubbish or tip it into a river, ditch or empty land.
Check with your host about a licensed waste service if your place has no collection.

V06.answer: Kalau melihat aturan adat Canggu, saat Nyepi ada empat pantangan yang dijalankan warga desa: tidak menyalakan api atau lampu, tidak bekerja, tidak bepergian, dan tidak membuat suara keras atau bersenang-senang. Aturan itu ditulis untuk warga desa adat setempat, jadi bukan kewajiban resmi Anda sebagai tamu. Tapi secara umum di Bali, tamu juga diharapkan ikut menjaga suasana hening: tinggal di dalam rumah, meredupkan lampu luar, dan tidak berpesta. Intinya, hari itu bukan waktunya jalan-jalan atau bersenang-senang. Sehari setelahnya, Ngembak Geni, aktivitas kembali normal dan orang saling memaafkan.
V06.why_it_matters: Nyepi adalah hari paling hening bagi umat Hindu Bali, saat semua aktivitas berhenti untuk bersemadi, dan ketenangan itu hanya terasa kalau semua orang di sekitar ikut menghormatinya.
recommended_actions: Tetap di dalam rumah atau kamar penginapan sepanjang hari Nyepi dan biarkan lampu luar tetap redup.

V10.answer: Yes, you should avoid stepping on it. Canang sari is a small daily offering made by Balinese Hindus, placed near homes, shops, shrines, entrances and sometimes on the pavement or road. It's part of everyday worship, not decoration or litter, so people here treat it with care. When you see one on the ground, simply walk around it where you can, and don't move, kick or disturb it. If you're not sure what something is or whether it's fine to pass, just ask your host or a local guide. Forms and meanings vary between offerings, so nobody expects you to read them all correctly.
V10.why_it_matters: Offerings sit at the centre of daily devotional life here, so treating them with quiet respect is one of the simplest ways to show respect to your Balinese neighbours.

Leave offerings where they are - don't move, kick or tidy them away
Ask your accommodation host or a local guide if you're unsure about an offering
Watch your step on pavements and shopfronts, where offerings are often placed

V11.answer: Galungan and Kuningan are two of the most important holy days in Balinese Hindu life — a celebration of devotion to God and the victory of dharma (goodness) over adharma (evil). You'll mostly notice the run-up: penjor (tall decorated bamboo poles) along the roads, offerings, families preparing, and businesses sometimes slowing down or changing hours. It's a genuinely religious occasion, not a festival staged for visitors. So the kind thing is to watch quietly from a respectful distance, ask your host or a local guide what's appropriate if you come across a ceremony, and simply go along with temporary changes to traffic, access or opening times. Villages also do things their own way, so don't expect everywhere to look the same.
V11.why_it_matters: For Balinese Hindus these days are about devotion and community rather than spectacle, and quiet respect is what people notice and appreciate.
recommended_actions: Ask your host or a local guide what is appropriate before joining or watching anything
Keep a respectful distance and stay out of the way during processions and worship
Expect and accept temporary changes to traffic, access and opening hours

You also need a valid driving licence that's recognised in Indonesia and valid for the vehicle you're riding, which for visitors usually means a national licence or an international driving permit for the right class. Carry your driving and vehicle documents, and rent from a properly registered rental business. The 2025 governor circular for foreign tourists restates these obligations, and Bali police have been actively checking helmets, phone use and wrong-way riding.
V13.why_it_matters: Helmets and proper paperwork keep you safe on Canggu's busy, narrow roads and keep things calm if you're waved over at a checkpoint — locals appreciate visitors who ride predictably and legally.

V20.answer: Early morning is usually your best bet — get there around first light and aim to be out of the water by mid-morning. In general in Bali, the wind is lightest at dawn, so the waves at Batu Bolong stay clean and glassy; by late morning the sea breeze picks up and it gets choppy and mushy. Mid tide tends to work well there, since it's a soft, friendly longboard wave that can get shallow at dead low. Afternoons are still surfable but messier, and the lineup gets busier through the day, so dawn also means fewer people competing for waves.

V24.answer: There are rules, and they apply right across Bali, Ubud included. A provincial government rule says nobody may enter a temple while in a state of ritual impurity (cuntaka or sebel), and nobody may go into a temple that isn't open for a ceremony or prayer unless they're directly involved in it. Damaging or desecrating a temple, its sacred images (pratima) or religious symbols is forbidden too. On top of that, each village and temple in Ubud can have its own customary rules, and I can't confirm those for you here.
V24.why_it_matters: Temples are the heart of village life in Bali, so keeping them pure and unharmed is how the community protects its relationship with the spiritual world and with each other.
recommended_actions: Ask your accommodation host or the temple's pemangku (the priest or keeper) about local rules before you visit a temple in Ubud.
Enter only when a temple is clearly open for worship, and dress and behave respectfully.
Stay outside if you think you might be in a state of impurity, and ask someone local rather than guessing.
Never touch, climb on or move shrines, sacred images or offerings.

H03.answer: No — single-use plastic bags are one of the items Bali's provincial rules single out as restricted, so shops shouldn't really be giving them out. The list also covers plastic straws, Styrofoam and plastic drink containers, and it applies to public places and waterways, not just beaches. In practice you'll still see them around, because how strictly this is followed varies from area to area and from shop to shop. The easy way to handle it is to carry a foldable tote and just say no thanks when a bag is offered — most people here appreciate it, and it keeps the island's rubbish problem from getting worse.
H03.why_it_matters: Bali's rivers and beaches are central to daily life and to ceremonies, so cutting plastic waste is something locals genuinely care about rather than just a rule on paper.
recommended_actions: Carry a reusable bag or tote whenever you shop or get takeaway
Politely decline a plastic bag if a shop offers one and use your own
Ask for paper, cardboard or reusable packaging where it's available

H04.answer: Ya, sebagai pengelola restoran di Canggu Anda termasuk pihak yang wajib mengelola sampah dengan benar. Aturan adat desa (pararem) di sini menyebut pengelola dan pegawai usaha harus mengurus sampahnya sendiri, terutama saat berada di area publik, dan wajib memilah sampah dengan baik. Kalau tidak memilah, usaha Anda bisa tidak mendapat layanan pengangkutan sampah dari unit pengelola sampah desa. Usaha juga bisa dilibatkan dalam kerja bakti (gotong royong) berkala di lingkungan desa adat. Jadi pastikan sampah restoran dipilah dan diserahkan lewat jalur pengangkutan yang benar.
H04.why_it_matters: Sampah yang dikelola rapi menjaga Canggu tetap nyaman dan bersih, dan menghormati aturan desa adat berarti ikut menjaga hubungan baik dengan warga sekitar.
recommended_actions: Pilah sampah restoran sesuai jenis yang diminta pengelola setempat, lalu simpan di tempat tertutup.
Tanyakan jadwal dan ketentuan pengangkutan sampah ke pengelola sampah desa atau banjar.
Ikuti gotong royong atau kerja bakti lingkungan bila usaha Anda dilibatkan.

H05.answer: Drive on the left in Bali. Keep to the left when joining traffic, turning or overtaking, and signal before you turn or change direction so the people around you can read what you're about to do. On narrow Canggu lanes this matters more than anywhere, because scooters, cars and pedestrians all share the same strip of road. If you're riding a scooter, wear a properly fastened helmet and keep your licence and vehicle documents with you. Use a phone only after you've stopped somewhere safe, and park where you're not blocking traffic or a footpath.
H05.why_it_matters: Predictable, left-side riding is what keeps crowded Balinese roads calm and safer for everyone who shares them, including pedestrians and cyclists.
recommended_actions: Ride and drive on the left, especially when pulling out of a side lane
Signal before every turn or lane change
Wear a fastened helmet and carry your licence and vehicle papers
Park only where you're not blocking traffic or a footpath

H06.answer: No — don't ride a scooter after drinking. Even one or two drinks is enough to make it unsafe and to put you in the wrong with the police, and Bali's rules for road users are clear that nobody should drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The same goes for helmets and licences: a short, quiet ride home doesn't make any of it optional. Locals take this seriously because so many people here ride, and everyone shares the same narrow roads. If you've been drinking, take a car with a driver, walk, or call a ride instead.
H06.why_it_matters: Most people here get around by scooter, so drink-riding is seen as a direct risk to neighbours and friends on the road, not just to yourself.
recommended_actions: Leave the scooter parked if you've had any alcohol.
Book a car with a driver or a ride app instead.
Always fasten your helmet properly, even for short trips.
Keep a valid licence for the vehicle class and carry your documents.

H08.answer: Tri Hita Karana is a Balinese way of describing a good life as three connected relationships: with the divine (parahyangan), between people (pawongan), and with the environment (palemahan). It is a broad framework people here use to talk about why temples, community ties and care for nature are linked rather than separate. Think of it as a lens for understanding Bali, not a rulebook. Different villages and institutions may emphasise it differently, so it is worth asking people you meet how they understand it where you are.
H08.why_it_matters: It helps you see why spiritual spaces, neighbourly obligations and looking after the land are treated as one connected whole in Balinese life.
recommended_actions: Keep the three relationships in mind when you visit temples, meet neighbours, or deal with rubbish and water.
Ask your host or a local guide how the idea is understood in your area of Canggu.
Treat it as a general guide to attitude, not a checklist of rules to follow.

H09.answer: I can't confirm current rates, but in general in Bali the safest bet is a bank branch or a properly licensed money changer (they display an official permit sign and count the notes out in front of you). Rates there are usually fair and close to the real exchange rate. Small street kiosks often advertise a rate that looks too good, then take a commission or a "fee" at the end, so it's worth comparing before you hand anything over. Bring your passport, ask for the total in rupiah before you agree, and count the money before you walk away.

R02.answer: Babi guling dan babi panggang itu dua hal berbeda. R02.why_it_matters: Babi guling bukan sekadar menu, tapi hidangan yang lekat dengan acara syukur dan upacara adat di Bali, jadi memesan atau menyantapnya terasa sedikit lebih istimewa.

R04.answer: In general in Bali, a warm smile and a simple greeting are the safest start. Say “Om Swastiastu” (a common Balinese Hindu greeting) or an Indonesian time-of-day greeting such as “Selamat pagi.” For a handshake, use your right hand and keep it gentle; with women, it’s polite to wait until she offers her hand first. Calling someone “Bapak” (Mr) or “Ibu” (Mrs) is respectful, especially with older people or staff. A slight nod and calm tone matter more than perfect words. Local habits differ between families and villages, so follow the lead of the person you’re meeting.
R04.why_it_matters: Greetings are a small but meaningful way to show respect and keep social harmony, which Balinese people generally value in everyday interactions.
recommended_actions: Start with a smile and a simple “Om Swastiastu” or “Selamat pagi.”
Use your right hand for handshakes and wait for a woman to offer hers first.
Address older people or staff as Bapak or Ibu.
Watch how locals greet each other and follow their lead.
